Late_blight.name: Late blight
Late_blight.spreads: Very fast in cool, wet, humid weather. Spores travel on wind and rain splash, and it can wipe out a tomato or potato crop within days.
look_for: Large dark, water-soaked patches on leaves
White fuzzy growth on the underside in humid mornings
Brown, greasy-looking lesions on stems
do_now: Remove affected leaves or whole plants, bag them, and take them off the field. Do not compost them.
Check every tomato and potato plant nearby today.
Avoid overhead watering and working among wet plants.
Ask your extension officer about a protective fungicide programme for the rest of the crop.
prevent: Space plants and prune for airflow
Use clean seed potatoes and resistant varieties
Destroy volunteer plants and cull piles

Early_blight.name: Early blight
Early_blight.spreads: Steadily, from the lower leaves upward, in warm humid weather. Spores survive on crop debris in the soil.
look_for: Brown spots with target-like rings on older, lower leaves
Yellowing around the spots
Leaves dropping from the bottom of the plant
do_now: Remove the spotted lower leaves and take them off the field.
Mulch the soil so rain doesn't splash spores onto leaves.
Water at the base of the plant, in the morning.
prevent: Rotate away from tomato, potato and pepper for 2 to 3 years
Keep plants well fed; stressed plants suffer most

Bacterial_spot.name: Bacterial spot
Bacterial_spot.spreads: With rain splash, wet hands, tools and contaminated seed or transplants, fastest in warm wet weather.
look_for: Small dark, greasy-looking spots on leaves, sometimes with a yellow halo
Spots merging into dead patches
Raised, scabby spots on fruit
do_now: Remove badly affected leaves and plants.
Stay out of the crop while it is wet.
Disinfect tools, and wash hands before touching healthy plants.
Ask your extension officer whether a copper-based spray is recommended locally.
prevent: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants

Leaf_Mold.name: Leaf mould
Leaf_Mold.spreads: Quickly in humid greenhouses and tunnels, much less in the open field.
look_for: Pale yellow patches on the upper leaf
Olive-green to brown velvety mould underneath
Leaves curling and dying from the bottom up
do_now: Improve ventilation and lower humidity (open vents, run fans).
Remove affected leaves.
Avoid wetting the leaves when watering.

Septoria_leaf_spot.name: Septoria leaf spot
Septoria_leaf_spot.spreads: From infected debris and lower leaves by rain splash, in warm wet weather.
look_for: Many small round spots with dark edges and grey-white centres
Tiny black dots in the spot centres
Lower leaves turning yellow and falling
do_now: Remove the spotted lower leaves.
Mulch, and water at the base.
Don't work among wet plants.

Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider_mite.name: Two-spotted spider mite
Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider_mite.spreads: Fast in hot, dry, dusty conditions. Mites move between plants on wind, clothing and tools.
look_for: Fine pale speckling on leaves
Fine webbing, mostly under leaves
Tiny moving dots under the leaf (use a hand lens)
do_now: Check the undersides of leaves on nearby plants.
Hose leaf undersides with water to knock mites off.
Remove heavily infested leaves.
Ask about miticides or predatory mites. Broad-spectrum insecticides can make mites worse by killing their predators.
prevent: Keep weeds down around the crop

Target_Spot.name: Target spot
Target_Spot.spreads: In warm, humid weather, especially in dense canopies.
look_for: Brown spots with light and dark rings on leaves
Spots also on stems and fruit
Leaves dropping in the dense middle of the plant
do_now: Remove affected leaves.
Prune to open the canopy to air.
Avoid overhead watering.

Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.spreads: By whiteflies, which carry it from plant to plant. There is no cure for an infected plant.
look_for: Leaves curling upward, small and yellow at the edges
Stunted, bushy growth
Flowers dropping and few fruit
do_now: Pull out infected plants, bag them, and remove them from the field.
Check the crop for whiteflies (shake a plant and watch).
Ask your extension officer about whitefly control.

Tomato_mosaic_virus.name: Tomato mosaic virus
Tomato_mosaic_virus.spreads: By touch: hands, tools, clothing and infected seed. It survives a long time on surfaces. There is no cure.
look_for: Light and dark green mottled (mosaic) leaves
Twisted or fern-like leaves
Stunted plants, uneven fruit colour
do_now: Remove infected plants, bagging them before carrying them out.
Wash hands with soap, and disinfect tools and stakes.
Work on healthy plants before sick ones.
Do not smoke or handle tobacco near the crop.
prevent: Use certified seed and resistant varieties
Disinfect tools and trays between crops

Apple_scab.name: Apple scab
Apple_scab.spreads: In spring rain, from spores in last season's fallen leaves.
look_for: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves
Dark scabby spots on fruit
Leaves yellowing and dropping early
do_now: Remove badly affected leaves and fruit.
Ask your extension officer about a spray schedule for wet periods.
prevent: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves in autumn

Black_rot.name: Black rot
Black_rot.cause: Fungus (Botryosphaeria on apple, Guignardia on grape)
Black_rot.spreads: From infected, shrivelled (mummified) fruit and dead wood, in warm wet weather.
look_for: Brown leaf spots with purple edges
Fruit rotting black and shrivelling
Sunken cankers on branches
do_now: Remove mummified fruit from the plant and the ground.
Prune out dead and cankered wood and take it away.
Ask your extension officer about protective sprays.
prevent: Clean up fruit and prunings every season

Cedar_apple_rust.name: Cedar apple rust
Cedar_apple_rust.spreads: Between apple trees and nearby junipers (cedars) in spring. It does not spread from apple to apple.
look_for: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf
Small tube-like growths underneath later on
do_now: Note which trees are affected; one outbreak is rarely serious.
Check for junipers nearby that carry the orange galls.

Powdery_mildew.name: Powdery mildew
Powdery_mildew.spreads: On wind, in warm days with humid nights. Unlike most fungi it doesn't need wet leaves.
look_for: White, flour-like powder on leaves and shoots
Leaves curling, yellowing or drying
do_now: Remove the worst-affected leaves.
Improve airflow around the plants.
Ask your extension officer about sulphur or other approved products.

Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_spot.name: Grey leaf spot (Cercospora)
Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_spot.spreads: From infected crop residue, in warm humid weather with long leaf wetness.
look_for: Long, narrow, rectangular grey-brown lesions between leaf veins
Lesions starting on the lower leaves
do_now: Scout the rest of the field to see how widespread it is.
Ask your extension officer whether a fungicide is worthwhile at this crop stage.
prevent: Bury or break down crop residue

Common_rust.name: Common rust
Common_rust.spreads: Spores blow in on the wind, in cool humid weather.
look_for: Small cinnamon-brown powdery pustules on both sides of the leaf
do_now: Scout the field; light rust rarely reduces yield.
Ask about treatment only if young plants are heavily covered.

Northern_Leaf_Blight.name: Northern leaf blight
Northern_Leaf_Blight.spreads: From infected residue, in moderate temperatures with heavy dew.
look_for: Long, cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions on the leaves
do_now: Scout the field to see how widespread it is.
Ask your extension officer whether treatment pays at this crop stage.

Esca_(Black_Measles).name: Esca (black measles)
Esca_(Black_Measles).spreads: Through pruning wounds, slowly, over years.
look_for: Tiger-stripe yellow or red patterns between leaf veins
Dark spots on berries
Vines suddenly wilting in summer
do_now: Mark the affected vines so they can be followed up.
Prune out dead wood and take it off the vineyard.

Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot).name: Grape leaf blight (Isariopsis leaf spot)
Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot).spreads: Mostly late in the season, in warm humid weather.
look_for: Dark red-brown irregular spots on leaves
Leaves drying and falling early
do_now: Remove affected leaves where practical.
Improve airflow in the canopy.

Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).name: Huanglongbing (citrus greening)
Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).cause: Bacteria, carried by the Asian citrus psyllid
Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).spreads: By psyllid insects and infected planting material. There is no cure, and in many countries it must be reported.
look_for: Blotchy, uneven yellowing across leaf veins
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the bottom
Tiny psyllid insects on new shoots
do_now: Report it to your agricultural department or extension officer; it may be a notifiable disease.
Do not move plant material off the farm.
Check new shoots for psyllids.
prevent: Buy only certified disease-free nursery trees

Leaf_scorch.name: Strawberry leaf scorch
Leaf_scorch.spreads: By rain splash, from infected old leaves.
look_for: Many small dark purple spots on leaves
Leaves looking burnt or scorched as spots merge
do_now: Remove affected old leaves.
Avoid overhead watering.
prevent: Renovate beds after harvest by removing old leaves
